title: Railway & Render
subtitle: Deploy Node.js, Python, and Docker backends with zero server management — databases included

content.text: Platform as a Service — the Heroku successors

Railway and Render are modern Platform as a Service (PaaS) providers — you give them your code or a Docker image, they handle everything else: provisioning servers, load balancing, auto-restart on crash, SSL, logging, and monitoring. Unlike EC2 (where you manage the OS) or ECS (where you manage container orchestration), PaaS requires near-zero ops knowledge. They're the fastest way to get a Node.js API or Python service into production with a real database.

content.code:
# Install Railway CLI
npm install -g @railway/cli

# Login
railway login

# Initialize a new project
railway init
# Or link to existing: railway link

# Deploy current directory
railway up
# Railway detects your framework automatically:
# - Node.js: runs 'npm start' (set in package.json)
# - Python: runs gunicorn or uvicorn
# - Dockerfile: builds and runs your container
# - No Dockerfile? Railway buildpacks detect your runtime

# Add a PostgreSQL database (one command):
railway add --plugin postgresql
# Sets DATABASE_URL in your environment automatically!

# Add Redis:
railway add --plugin redis
# Sets REDIS_URL automatically

# Run a one-off command (migrations, seeds):
railway run npm run db:migrate

# View logs:
railway logs

# Open your deployed app:
railway open

# Environment variables:
railway variables set NODE_ENV=production
railway variables set JWT_SECRET=mysecretkey
railway variables list

# render.yaml in your repo root
# Defines all your services declaratively

services:
  # Web service (your Node.js API)
  - type: web
    name: myapp-api
    runtime: node
    plan: starter  # $7/month, or 'free' (sleeps after 15min inactive)
    buildCommand: npm ci && npm run build
    startCommand: npm start
    healthCheckPath: /health
    envVars:
      - key: NODE_ENV
        value: production
      - key: DATABASE_URL
        fromDatabase:
          name: myapp-db
          property: connectionString
      - key: JWT_SECRET
        generateValue: true  # Render generates a random secret

  # Background worker
  - type: worker
    name: myapp-worker
    runtime: node
    buildCommand: npm ci
    startCommand: node workers/email.js
    envVars:
      - fromService:
          name: myapp-api
          type: web
          envVarKey: DATABASE_URL

databases:
  - name: myapp-db
    plan: starter  # $7/month for persistent PostgreSQL
    databaseName: myapp
    user: myapp

RAILWAY:
  Pricing: Pay for what you use (usage-based, not plans)
           ~$0.000231/vCPU-minute, ~$0.0000128/MB-minute
           $5 free credit/month on Hobby plan
  Database: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB as plugins
  DX:       Best-in-class — 'railway up' is 1 command deploy
  Best for: Rapid prototyping, startups, any language/framework
  No sleep: Services stay awake always (unlike Render free tier)

RENDER:
  Pricing:  Starter web service: $7/month
            Free tier: web services (sleep after 15min)
  Database: Managed PostgreSQL, Redis
  DX:       render.yaml IaC, GitHub auto-deploy
  Best for: Simpler projects, teams wanting predictable pricing
  Free tier: Good for personal projects that tolerate cold starts

BOTH:
  ✓ Automatic HTTPS
  ✓ GitHub/GitLab deploy on push
  ✓ Environment variables
  ✓ PostgreSQL and Redis
  ✓ Custom domains
  ✓ Zero server management

HEROKU COMPARISON:
  Railway and Render are what Heroku used to be before price changes
  Both offer better value and similar or better DX

content.text: Render's free tier web services sleep after 15 minutes of inactivity. When the first request arrives after sleeping, the service cold-starts (taking 30-60 seconds). This is fine for personal projects and portfolios. For anything with real users, use a paid tier or keep the service awake with a periodic ping (a health check every 10 minutes). Railway's free tier doesn't sleep, but has $5/month credit limits.

questions.question: You add a PostgreSQL plugin to Railway. Where does the DATABASE_URL connection string go?
options: You must manually copy it from the Railway dashboard and add it to your .env file
Railway automatically injects DATABASE_URL as an environment variable into all services in the same project
The connection string is stored in a separate config file you must reference
Railway emails you the connection string
questions.explanation: Railway automatically injects service variables (like DATABASE_URL from a PostgreSQL plugin) into all services in the same project. Your Node.js code reads process.env.DATABASE_URL — no manual configuration needed. This is Railway's 'service variables' feature: any variable a plugin service exposes is automatically available to all other services in the project. It's one of the reasons Railway's DX is so smooth.

faq.q: Should I use Railway/Render or AWS for my startup?
faq.a: Start with Railway or Render. They're 10x faster to get running, require no AWS knowledge, and cost $5-20/month for a typical small app. Migrate to AWS when: you need specific AWS services (SQS, Lambda at scale, custom VPC networking), your bill exceeds $100/month and AWS would be cheaper, or you need compliance certifications that AWS has but PaaS doesn't. Most startups are on PaaS until well after product-market fit.

examples: Dozens of YC startups ship their initial product on Railway. The ability to have a full backend + database running in < 5 minutes lets teams validate products faster — infrastructure isn't the bottleneck
Pocketbase, Supabase, and many developer tool companies run their own deployments on Railway for dogfooding and demos — Railway's simplicity makes it easy to spin up isolated environments
